brief.head: The university waqf
brief.text: A waqf set up to build water fountains keeps its capital after piped water arrives. Universities’ vast endowments, Amit Varma said, are much the same: dead capital. {024-C13}

brief.head: Write it, think it
brief.text: Writing clearly is not just a sign of clear thinking, Amit Varma said after George Orwell. Forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly. {024-C11}

brief.head: Let firms fund it
brief.text: Corporations make meritocratic funders of research, Ajay Shah said, because they pose concrete problems. Government funding is a state-capacity problem; philanthropy plays too safe. {024-C03}

brief.head: Who are we, anyway?
brief.text: Firms and governments must keep asking who they are and what they are doing wrong, Ajay Shah said. Too often they become contests for power. {024-C06}

brief.head: Communities of choice
brief.text: Toxic as Twitter is, Amit Varma said, it lets him watch the best minds think aloud every morning. Most of his friends he met because of the internet. {024-C14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on knowledge and its keepers
lead.head: The academy fails its own exam
body: Ajay Shah, Amit Varma said, likes to tease him for having studied nothing while Shah is a card-carrying economist with a PhD. Yet here Shah was, agreeing that academics is broken and degrees mean nothing. “Across twenty short episodes,” Shah said, “Amit has changed my views.” {024-J01}
The subject was the knowledge society, and why its institutions are failing.

Knowledge, Shah said, is “the great nuclear reactor running inside the entire modern world”. Every knowledge organisation, he argued, has a three-part mission. “So we are here to make knowledge, to diffuse knowledge, and to link up knowledge to action to translate knowledge into a better world.” {024-C01}
All three pillars, he said, are a little broken.
## Three cracks

On the making of knowledge, Shah described a profession that has traded curiosity for career ladders. The question is no longer what important problem one can solve, but how to get into a particular journal.

In economics, which he called the most broken journal process of all, an idea that took a week can take five to eight years to publish. “People probably get three good days a year of imagining,” he said, “and three hundred and sixty-two days a year are just spent on mundane shit of schmoozing, of networking, of figuring out what editors like, what referees like.” {024-C02}
Most published papers, he added, are never cited.
On the spreading of knowledge, the university has become a brand-name factory. Students want the degree that gets them a job at Google. Parents get four years of daycare; employers get a signal.
The brand itself adds little, Shah said. “If you take any IIT graduate, and if they did not attend IIT, you know what, their life would more or less be the same.”
Nor can learning be crammed into four years, he said, when people live longer and the world keeps changing.
## The view from outside
Varma, who said he was not a creature of that world, put it more bluntly. “I think academics is utterly irrelevant. It’s a circle jerk. It’s pompous old farts talking to other pompous old farts.”
He took aim at turgid prose, at silos and at conformity.
But he was not in despair. Anyone with hunger can now learn from YouTube, podcasts and books, and creators own the means of production.
“We are playing the long game, we are building a repository of content, and we are trying to create in different ways a community of thinkers,” he said. {024-C16}
His imagined viewer is a fifteen-year-old girl in a remote Indian town who will be prime minister in thirty years.
## Mind the selectors

Shah’s parting thought came from cricket. A player’s worth matters only once it reaches the selectors, and in academia, he said, the deepest failures lie in who gets selected, promoted and funded. {024-C07}
Admissions reward regimentation and good grades rather than curiosity, and the result is safe, bureaucratic people instead of an Einstein or a Ramanujan.

He also argued that credit is widely shared, and that winner-takes-all prizes make people hoard ideas. Varma, twice a winner of the Bastiat Prize, wanted a free market in prizes rather than none. “But do not take my two candlesticks away from me,” he said.

second.label: Einstein’s day job
second.head: A clerk with no budget
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s model researcher was a patent clerk with zero funding
body: Ajay Shah’s ideal of how knowledge should be made is Albert Einstein, a full-time clerk in a patent office. “Just imagine he’s doing a day job in a patent office, he can’t be very well paid and he has zero budgets, he has no funding,” Shah said. Einstein became one of the most influential scientists ever. {024-S02}
Shah apologised to viewers who work in patent offices. His point was that Einstein, like Ramanujan, was driven by an inner hunger: curiosity and passion, pursued for their own sake.

Modern academics is instead a game of climbing career ladders, chasing journal publications and funding. So, Shah said, “we get dull people joining, or bright people have the spark smashed out of them”. {#spark}

quote.text: We want thinkers and intellectuals who have their inner fire of curiosity and of passion

third.head: Knowledge in every pore
body: Ajay Shah remembers a speech by Vajpayee, from around 2002 or 2003, with some beautiful paragraphs on the knowledge economy. Its message was that knowledge is not something to hide in a university. {024-S01}

“The knowledge economy should fill every pore of our bodies,” Shah recalled. Knowledge should cast aside superstition in individual lives. It should feed into firms, making them high-productivity firms, and into the state, so that it practises evidence-based policy.
Shah set this against a crude view of politics found in India: you win elections, and then you send agencies after your rivals. That view, he conceded, has a germ of truth in it.
The power-and-coercion view of the state, he said, “is a royal road to ruin. And that is what underdevelopment and the third world is all about.” {#ruin}
third.caption: Vajpayee’s knowledge speech

p2.title: The knowledge society
p2.deck: How knowledge is made, spread and put to use, and why the hosts think creators are taking over {024-C01}

sections.label: Pillar One
sections.head: Shut up and get the pub
sections.caption: the journal game
body: Ajay Shah has spent more years in universities than he cares to admit, and he wanted the hosts to turn the analytical lens on themselves. If they can make fun of homeopathy and hydroponics, he said, they should make fun of academia too.

Much of the world’s knowledge, he said, is shaped by journals and funding. Researchers no longer ask what important problem they can solve; they study what editors and referees like, “a bit like lemmings”.

The irony, Shah said, is that papers in the top-ranked journals are in many ways the less good ones, because more energy went into hacking the system. Of all fields, he thinks economics has the most broken journal process. {024-C02}
## Publication orientation

Young researchers meet a dreaded phrase, “publication orientation”, which older academics use to beat the idealism out of them. “You’re supposed to organize your life around shut up and get the pub,” Shah said. {024-J14}
Funding works best, he argued, when it comes from corporations, which are meritocratic and pose concrete problems, such as making a widget work at 256 degrees. {#widget}

~ Philanthropy, by contrast, chases feel-good goals and plays safe. “James Watt arguably did more for poor people in India than Mother Teresa,” Shah said. “But most philanthropists are not sufficiently intellectual to see these links.” {024-C03}

quote.text: It stopped becoming what’s an important problem that I can solve. It’s become how do I hack into X journal and get that paper.

sections.label: Pillar Two
sections.head: Four years of daycare
sections.caption: credentialism and lifelong learning
body: The diffusion of knowledge, Ajay Shah said, has degenerated into credentialism. Students have no interest in the knowledge; they want the degree that gets them a job with Google.

Universities have noticed what their brand names are worth, and their prices have crept up. The hosts’ friend Josh Felman told Shah that putting one child through college in America “involves buying one brand new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff”. {024-J04}
The money buys gyms, luxurious housing and five-star facilities. Students are made to work 12 hours a day in regimented ways, which, Shah said, breeds mediocrity. {#twelve}
The real bargain: parents get daycare for four years, the children get a *chapa*, a stamp, and a job follows.
## Kindling, not filling
Learning, for Shah, never finishes. He offered “a beautiful quotation”: “the process of education is not filling a pail, the process of education is kindling a fire.” {024-J15}

The university is an industrial-era construct, he said, from when people stopped work at 55 or 60. The hosts had told their cameraman Vaishnav that he would live to 120, and over a hundred years, everything about him will change. {#vaishnav}
~ Even the hosts, Shah noted, had to learn at a ripe age what it means to make a YouTube show.

quote.text: I can display formal competence. I can pass any exam, but I’ve not actually understood things.

sections.label: The outsider’s view
sections.head: Turgid by design
sections.caption: turgid prose and conformity
body: Amit Varma’s writing students often ask what to do about the turgid prose academia expects of them. He points them to an essay by the philosopher Agnes Callard, *Publish and Perish*, which explains it with an economist’s tool: incentives. {024-R05}
Tenure requires publications in certain journals, and those journals reward their own conventions, turgid writing among them, along with the intellectual fashions of the day.

Varma’s advice has two parts. Clear academic writing is possible, so find models such as the economists Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok. And if a career demands the style, use it knowingly and keep it out of everything else. {024-C10}
## Wheat in Arizona
His other complaints are silos and conformity. Dig deep enough, he said, and “you’ll be writing about wheat production in Arizona between the years 1863 to 1865”. {024-J07}

Young people arrive as self-declared rebels and conform anyway. A paper by Paul Smaldino and Joshua Epstein puts it in its title: *Social Conformity Despite Individual Preferences for Distinctiveness*. {024-R07}

~ The cure, for Varma, is many frames and a multidisciplinary outlook, the motto behind the show’s name. “If you are in the business of knowledge, then you cannot have one frame, one hammer for every nail.” {024-C12}

quote.text: But know why you’re doing it and don’t let those habits seep into the other writing that you do.

sections.label: The golden age
sections.head: No gatekeeper required
sections.caption: the creator’s golden age
body: For most of history, Amit Varma said, your knowledge was limited to what the people around you told you. Even after Gutenberg, only a small elite read, and universities made sense as places where knowledge and bright minds gathered.
Not any more. Anyone with the hunger and the spark can learn from YouTube, podcasts and books. Varma said he had told Vaishnav that he wished he were fifteen today. {#fifteen}

Spreading what you knew used to mean passing gatekeepers, with their biases, their scarce space and their budgets. Now creators own the means of production, and niches no one knew existed can suddenly appear.
## Ninety-five per cent
Sniffiness about popular YouTubers misses Sturgeon’s Law, Varma said: “Ninety five percent of everything is crap,” and it has always been so. {024-J19}
Ajay Shah added a thought on the self-taught genius: “Today, Ramanujan would have been doling out his gems, one blog article at a time.” {024-J10}
~ Varma agreed. Ramanujan, he said, had to rediscover things that were already known, and with access to knowledge he might have learned faster.

quote.text: You no longer need to say XYZ is bad. That sucks. You can now say sure XYZ is bad, so what? I’ll do better.

sections.label: The long game
sections.head: Picasso had help
sections.caption: credit, prizes and selectors
body: Ajay Shah borrowed a lesson from cricket. A player’s value becomes a programme for action only when it reaches the selectors, and in academia, too, the root cause lies with those who select, promote and fund. {024-C07}
Admissions demand regimentation and good grades, and India’s populist insistence on objective exams makes things worse. The best people, he said, are not coming into the knowledge business.
## The last runner
Credit, Shah argued, is dispersed. Picasso did not step out of thin air and invent cubism; he picked up pieces from the many people around him. {#picasso}
Prizes reward only the runner who takes the baton across the finish line. “If you and I are in a race for a Nobel Prize, then I’ll be hoarding my ideas and you’ll be hoarding your ideas.” {024-C08}
He would extend authorship even to someone met once at a bicycle repair shop, if the conversation shaped the paper.
Amit Varma, who has won the Bastiat Prize twice, answered with competition rather than abolition: let anyone fund a prize for whatever they value. {024-C09}
~ Shah quoted a songwriter both hosts think a lot about: “and I won and I won big once. And I paid the cost.” {024-J17}

quote.text: So that one who wins big should be seen in the context of all the other strivers.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah thinks all three pillars of a knowledge society are a little broken. They are to make knowledge, to diffuse it, and to turn it into a better world through firms and the state. That, he said, should be every university trustee’s mission statement. {024-C01}

contQuote.text: It takes years of dedication and attention and focus and a passion for knowing, through which, bit by bit the veils part and the universe reveals its knowledge to you.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A mathematician, a podcaster, a prize-winner and Adam Smith’s bookshelf

stories.start: I want to tell a little story about a great mathematician.
stories.end: I don't want to do this. So he never appeared for the prize.
stories.caption: Grigori Perelman’s refusal
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a mathematician who said no to everything
stories.head: A proof needs no prize
body: Grigori Perelman, as Ajay Shah tells it, is a great mathematician and a charming guy. He lives in Moscow with his mother, and walks in the forest gathering mushrooms.
He also did some great work, which, Shah said, would take many minutes to explain. Perelman wrote a paper and put it up on a website, arXiv, and was done.

Why not publish it in a journal, people asked. Perelman’s reply, in Shah’s telling: “Either the proof is right or the proof is wrong. If the proof is right, I am a good mathematician and for hundreds of years this will be remembered. If the proof is wrong, this stuff should just be thrown away.” {024-S05}
A journal’s brand name, he reasoned, could make no difference to the quality of the work. If people liked the paper, they would read it.
Then came fame, and prizes. The organisers of a Clay award of a million dollars quietly asked whether he would come and collect it. He said no. They asked again. He said no again.

Prizes, he explained, give excessively disproportionate rewards to some people and damage the collaboration DNA of the whole community. He had stood on the shoulders of many others who got no prize. And he lived with his mother, walked in the forest and collected mushrooms. What would he do with a million dollars?

~ He never appeared for the prize. Shah’s own worry about prizes, he said, was an idea he stole from Perelman, who opened his eyes to how one person’s award leaves everyone else a little in the shadow. {#stole}
stories.why: Perelman cut out both middlemen of academic credit, the journal and the prize. For Shah, his refusal shows how winner-takes-all rewards reshape everyone else’s incentives and damage the collaboration on which knowledge depends. {024-C08}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma called it a “magnificent inspiring story”, and then, as a two-time prize winner, begged to differ.

stories.caption: the eight-hour podcast
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on writing before and after the gatekeepers
stories.head: No editor, no word limit
body: In the 1990s, Amit Varma said, a writer with something to say sent an article to a newspaper like the *Times of India* or the *Hindustan Times*. The paper sold readers’ eyeballs to advertisers, and the writer got a tiny chunk of the money.
Then Varma became one of the early bloggers. He no longer needed a gatekeeper, a news cycle or a limit of 800 or 900 words, and he could talk directly with readers. {#words}

Thirty years ago, he said, he would have gone to a radio company, the only audio there was, and proposed an eight-hour podcast of long conversations with boring academics. “I would have been laughed out of the room.” {024-S04}
~ Today he is a professional podcaster, and all the money he makes comes directly from listeners and viewers.
stories.why: Creators now own the means of production for ideas. Formats nobody imagined can find an audience without asking a gatekeeper’s permission, and the money can come straight from the people who listen. {024-C15}

stories.start: I have won something called the Bastiard Prize twice.
stories.end: But sometimes I feel that things like this can be useful.
stories.caption: his two Bastiat Prizes
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the award that kept him going
stories.head: Lonely road, two prizes
body: The Bastiat Prize, named after Amit Varma’s hero Frédéric Bastiat, goes to a journalist who upholds the ideals of a free society. Varma first won it in 2007, when, he said, he was literally the only person in India writing about freedom.
“It was a lonely journey,” he said. “Everybody abused me in those days.” The $10,000 that came with the prize meant a lot to him too. {#tenk}

Then he renounced the world for five years to play poker, and came back to find everyone had forgotten him. He started writing again and won the prize again in 2015, the first person, he said, to win it twice. {024-S06}
~ He would never take a government award, and the Khan Market Liberal Award, he said, “will never be accepted by me”. {024-J11}
stories.why: A prize can sustain a lonely contrarian instead of rewarding conformity. Varma’s answer to elite awards is not to abolish prizes but to have many of them, competing, so that lonely voices can be recognised. {024-C09}

stories.end: his thinking is remarkable, to me that makes his achievement even greater.
stories.caption: Adam Smith’s turgid prose
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on judging a thinker by his library
stories.head: What did Adam Smith read?
body: Amit Varma’s writing students sometimes ask why Adam Smith, one of his great heroes, writes prose that can be a bit turgid at times. {024-S03}

Varma’s answer is to look at what Smith had to work with. Gutenberg had brought the printing press and books, but it was still a small number of elites who read. Anyone setting out to gain and make knowledge had a very small sample to work with.
“Think of what he must have read. Think of the models he would have had,” Varma said. Smith had no world of literature on writing, and no writing courses like Varma’s.
~ Yet the ideas Smith came up with are remarkable, and to Varma that makes his achievement even greater.
stories.why: Judge thinkers by what they had to read. Smith built remarkable ideas from a tiny sample; today anyone with hunger can learn anything, which is why Varma wishes he were fifteen now. {#fifteen}

quiz.q: What full-time job did Albert Einstein hold while becoming one of the most influential scientists?
quiz.a: He was a clerk in a patent office, with no research funding.

quiz.q: According to Josh Felman, what is putting one child through an American college like?
quiz.a: Buying a brand new BMW every year and rolling it off a cliff.

quiz.q: Why did Grigori Perelman refuse to publish his proof in a journal?
quiz.a: A proof is right or wrong; a journal’s brand name changes nothing.

quiz.q: Which essay by Agnes Callard explains why academic writing is so turgid?
quiz.a: *Publish and Perish*, which blames the incentives of tenure and journals.

quiz.q: What did Timur Kuran’s waqfs teach Amit Varma about university endowments?
quiz.a: Like waqfs whose mission has lapsed, they sit on largely dead capital.

quiz.q: Who is the imagined viewer Amit Varma hopes will learn from the show?
quiz.a: A fifteen-year-old girl in a remote Indian town, a future prime minister.
